translations.text: The Triumphs of Mar Rabbula, Bishop of the Blessed City of Edessa.
My brothers, with zeal for the love of Christ, we portray before you, beloved, through writing, an image of the virtuous deeds
of Mar Rabbula the bishop, the pride of our city, so that he may be for us and for all generations an inspiring example, whose good deeds we may emulate.
He proved himself a mighty contestant in the arena of righteousness and was victorious in fierce battles against the principalities.
He overcame the cunning of the Accuser through his wisdom. With discernment he despised the world and its desires, and through his prowess in battle he trampled the enemy’s power.
He subdued the body and its passions through his endurance. He overcame Satan, his adversary, in combat, and brought those whom Satan had led astray back to his truth.
Through the keenness of his endurance he subdued the cunning devices of sin’s sweet enticements. He helped people through his words,
and benefited many through his deeds. He delighted and astonished the angels through his perseverance. He glorified and magnified his Lord through his faith, and saved his soul
and spent his life. The Spirit of God rested in him throughout his life, until from all the contests of self-denial he won the crown of uprightness,
adorned with a good end worthy of God. Therefore, for this man of illustrious renown,
we ought, as a duty, to record a cherished remembrance of his godly conduct, so that the image of his triumphs may be for us and for all generations
an inspiring example for them to emulate, as with the virtuous fathers of illustrious renown,
whose virtues are portrayed in the Old and New Testaments, embodied through the written words of the Holy Scriptures as through pigments.
Now this blessed Rabbula was a pagan from his childhood, because his father too was a pagan and a priest. And the wicked Julian
is said to have offered himself to the demons through this man’s own hands when he was setting out to war against the Persians. His mother, however, was a believer.
She constantly struggled with her husband to turn him to the worship of Christ, but she could not turn the force of his tyrannical will toward the truth.
He too tried in every way to entice this believing woman, but he could not enslave to sin the strength of her freedom in Jesus.
Each of them therefore remained in their own beliefs. From them was born Rabbula the zealous, triumphant in everything, a second Josiah,
if this likeness is sufficient for us to portray the saint’s honor. His mother entrusted him to a believing nurse to suckle him.
When he grew up, he was educated in Greek literature, as the son of a very wealthy family in their city of Chalcis. His mother had already obtained for him
a believing wife. His wife and his mother constantly urged him to turn from his father’s paganism to faith in Christ, but he would not be persuaded by them.
He took pride in the distinguished authority of the office bestowed on him by the emperor. Then a favorable occasion arose for him to travel to his villages
toward the desert of Chalcis. Within the boundaries of one of his estates there was a renowned monastery belonging to the blessed Abraham the recluse.
His servants and the inhabitants of that region would tell him, “Brothers who are strangers live in this monastery,
and astonishing miracles of healing are performed through their hands by Christ, the God of the Christians.” And when he heard this,
The report of his signs amazed him when he heard it, and the news of his victories poured into his soul like oceans.
As the fire of love for this worshipful name of Jesus spread through his heart, his mind began to question his paganism.
Quickly and urgently, through God's providence, it brought him to see this blessed man,
so that he might see with his own eyes the power of the miracles of Jesus, toward whom he had been hostile, just as Jesus had been persecuted by Paul at the beginning.
With the lash of a heavenly voice, he came and yoked him to the yoke of the cross as he bowed in worship, and snatched him from Judaism into his truth,
just as he also brought Rabbula from paganism to Christianity. And because signs are absolutely necessary for those who do not believe,
that good Lord, who cares for his servants, prepared beforehand a catch for life, as he had for the Samaritan woman
and Nathanael, through a small sign by which he was caught for life. He arranged for a woman to come before the victorious Abraham,
whose flesh was wasting away and whose limbs were paralyzed from a severe illness of long duration. When the blessed Rabbula saw this miracle,
he went away marveling inwardly at what had happened, and through the power of Christ he began to question his paganism. In his heart he said to himself,
as he himself used to tell us, “If you think it a disgrace to renounce the shameful gods of the Greeks and acknowledge a crucified God,
look at what the remembrance of his cross has done within your soul through the healing of that woman, and set yourself free.”
When his mother saw that his complexion had changed, and heard from those who had been with him about the divine deed performed before his eyes,
she hurried in her joy and went to the blessed Eusebius, the bishop of her city. She told him what had happened to her son and [?].
Since he was still evasive, even though he had explained many things to him from the Scriptures about Christ, he thought that help from others would lend support to his words.
For this reason he got up, eagerly took him along, and brought him to the illustrious Acacius, bishop of the city of Aleppo.
For they were brothers in Christ and had been trained together in the venerable life of the monastery.
When Acacius heard the reason for their coming, he rejoiced greatly. His affection for Rabbula became apparent, and he began to say to him, “My son,
you cannot understand the power of the truth—that it is truth—unless you recognize that this thing
you know is error.” But he answered him, “How can I know
that what I know is error unless truth itself, through its light, clearly shows me truth and error?”
Acacius acknowledged the force of this reply and said to him, “You can indeed know the truth
if you recognize that you do not yet know it.” But Rabbula said, “Knowing that I do not know the truth
does not make the truth known to me. It only convinces me that my error is error. But it is the truth itself that I want to know.”
Acacius said to him, “Believe in our Lord Jesus, who is the Son of God, and the truth knows how to draw you to itself.”
But he said, “How can I come to know Christ? For if he is the certain truth, I must know him.”
Eusebius said to him, “The truth himself will make himself known to you, if you empty yourself of your own knowledge and acquire a need to know him.”
Rabbula said, “And how can I forget these things, which I remember even against my will?” Eusebius said:
“When you bring the constant remembrance of Jesus to dwell within you, all the evil things that fight against you will see him and flee from you,
just as darkness withdraws before rays of light.” After they had spoken at length with one another about the faith, he vowed to go and pray
at the shrine of the glorious martyrs Cosmas and Damian. They equipped him with prayer and joyfully sent him on his way. While he was standing in the church, he saw a man he knew
who had been blind and now could see. He marveled at the power of the cross, but he was even more amazed at the miracle God performed in his own person:
the Lord opened his lips, and he offered new praise, praise to God—to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
He gave alms there, moved by what he had seen and heard. Then he went back on his way, despising himself for the error in which he had lived until then.
He came to Acacius and told him how, as he stood praying, God had caused praise to shine forth from his mouth.
He confessed his faith in Jesus before him. When Acacius heard this, he rejoiced in his faith and said to him, “My son,
when the fire of love for God courses through someone's heart, all desires, together with all the thickets of sin, are scorched and burned up in it.
And he himself is purified sevenfold through them and made white.” Then the bishops Acacius and Eusebius took him to the monastery of the holy recluse Marcian,
and to the blessed Abraham whom we mentioned above. With abundant words they strengthened his resolve and urged him to stay.
Rabbula promised them, saying, “Because I have truly placed my hope in the Lord and believed in the Son of God,
I have vowed my whole self to God. I will leave the world entirely, follow God completely, and shut myself away in a monastery like you.
And this is my desire: to go to Jerusalem, see the holy place, and be baptized in the Jordan, where Christ himself was baptized as an example for us.”
When the fathers heard these things, they rejoiced. They equipped him with prayer and sent him on his way. When he entered Jerusalem,
the blessed Mar Rabbula prayed before Golgotha with many tears and sorrow. He entered the tomb of our Lord and the cave in which he was born, and went up to the place of the Ascension.
He gave alms to the poor and went down from there to the Jordan. At once he appealed to the priests and recited the faith before them. They anointed him and baptized him.
As soon as he came up from the water, the linen cloth wrapped around his body, according to the custom of Christ's spiritual bridegrooms, was seen gleaming all over, on every side,
with the unique dye of Christ's blood in the form of crosses. When all those there saw this great miracle,
they saw and marveled and were shaken, and trembling seized them. In their agitation they fell down and knelt in prayer before God.

With loud voices they praised God for all the mighty deeds they had seen. After he had partaken of the holy mysteries of our Lord's body and blood and had been made complete in the whole divine mystery,
he returned to his city, rejoicing in his faith, exulting in his hope, delighting in his love, and intoxicated with his affection.
and receives the grace of God. As soon as the blessed Rabbula had been baptized, he went down to his city, entered his house, and acted according to the commitment he had made in his vow.
Like a wise merchant who goes out looking for fine pearls, when he found the pearl he had hoped for,
he went and sold everything he had and bought it. For he distributed his gold, his silver, and everything he owned to the needy.
His almsgiving reached even the holy people and the poor of Edessa, the city that, in his prophetic foresight, he was destined to receive
as his inheritance. For the mystery of Christ had already betrothed her to him through the pledge of his almsgiving,
through her poor members, just as he had done for the other regions. For he discerningly recognized within himself that the attractions of this world and preoccupation with wealth
choke the seed of the word of God like brushwood and thorns in a soul that is not watchful, and it bears no fruit.
For this reason he eagerly cast off the whole crushing weight of the bonds of wealth, so that the word of God he had received might readily flourish in his inner being
and bear fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold. So he joyfully accepted our Lord’s command: “Whoever does not renounce all his possessions
cannot be my disciple.” He diligently scattered abroad and gave everything he owned to the poor, so that his righteousness might endure forever.
He also sold his estates and distributed their entire price to the needy, so that through their hands his deposits might be brought into the heavenly treasury,
and his treasures, together with their gains, might be kept there for him. As for his slaves, both those born in his household and those bought with his money,
he freed them all. He provided each one with supplies and sent him away in peace. Some of them he instructed, made disciples, and brought into monasteries.
He took away all that his blessed mother owned, while she rejoiced, and she took up the yoke of Christ. He did the same for his wife.
While his sons were still children, he made them disciples and entrusted them to monasteries. Thus he emptied himself of everything he owned, so that he might gain the Lord of all possessions.
When, according to our Lord’s command, he had separated himself from his mother and his wife, from his sons and his daughters, from his estates and all his possessions, from his foods and from
his slaves, from his friends and everything the world possesses, he took up his cross inwardly, according to our Lord’s command, and followed him wholeheartedly.
As soon as he had stripped himself, while still alive, of the world and everything in it, he went out alone into the wilderness with the burning desire of his true love for Christ,
so that he too might be tempted by the devil, following our Lord’s example, and might engage in combat with savage passions like mighty warriors in the wilderness,
and grapple with nature and its habits, and fight like a spiritual athlete against principalities and powers
and against evil spirits, within and without. He went and lived in the wilderness monastery of the blessed Abraham, whom we mentioned above.
Through a small gleam from one of Abraham’s signs, the blessed Rabbula had first been drawn out of the darkness of paganism into the light of truth.
After he had lived with him for some time, practicing great acts of asceticism, he urged him to take a small dwelling nearby and pursue his way of life there at ease.
He yielded to his persuasion and took charge of a monastery. His brother and others lived with him,
along with the blessed Eusebius, whom the holy Rabbula had made bishop in Tella, the city renowned for its names.
Their way of life, as in all the monasteries, was modeled on the church of the apostles: everything they had was held in common.
For often, when they had no food, they passed the night rejoicing.
One day, as usual, the bread ran out in their monastery. While he was thanking his Lord for finding him worthy to endure
such sufferings with joy, grace sent them the bread they needed at sunset.
But marvel and be amazed at the strength of mind of the blessed Rabbula. For he saw this act of grace and said:
“Because God has recognized my weakness, that I cannot endure afflictions, he has done this to test me.”
With this judgment, he took that food and gave it to others that evening, and they themselves went to bed hungry.
When he saw that people had begun flocking to him as to a man who had abandoned the world and loved solitude,
hated himself and loved God, so that he would not be held back by their attention from the unceasing course of his righteousness,
he slipped away from them and moved into the inner desert, as the blessed Antony had also done. He found a small cave in the ground,
and beside it a spring of water that trickled enough for one person. His only occupation there was this: constant prayer,
the service of psalms, and the reading of the Scriptures. For these are the righteous rules appropriate to all monasteries and to everyone who belongs to our Lord.
Indeed, this was also why he went there: so that meditation on God would never cease in his soul. For there the evil one stirred up against him
all his many and varied assaults, as the blessed man himself related. A terrifying swarm of many forms
fought openly against him. For he made snakes and scorpions swarm around him and above him to frighten him,
and vipers and [?] to terrify him. They were all defeated by the power of the sign of the cross. When Satan could not prevail by his power, the jar
of water he would overturn, for that little spring dripped out only enough to meet his need. But these things with which Satan fought fiercely against him to make him suffer
became abundant resources for his great righteousness, so that he would apply himself diligently to prayer,
plead, and cry out mightily to God to deliver him from every evil. For through endurance, both inward and outward, he struggled resolutely against the evil one.
He was ready to meet every evil impulse with every good impulse and to prevail.
While he was standing in prayer so that his communion with God would not be interrupted, suddenly a band of Arab raiders appeared, coming toward him.
He rejoiced, thinking that the time for his crowning had already arrived. But they saw a living dead man in an empty hollow,
and they scorned him and left him alone. They took only his bread and his covering and went away. He thanked his Lord even for this.
But marvel at this: they encountered a man who was coming to bring him a gift of bread for his needs, and they did not harm him,
so that his endurance might triumph in both circumstances. And while he was living this angelic way of life in body and soul:
And he kept his mind dwelling before God, like the angels in their service in heaven. The members of his monastery learned where he was and how he was living.
They came and persuaded him to return with them. But the desire to confess his faith was burning like fire in his heart.
He arose and took the blessed Eusebius with him. The two of them traveled to Baalbek, the city of the pagans, and entered the temple of their idols,
in their zeal for God, to break them and be found worthy of martyrdom. For they did not go there expecting to return alive,
but in the hope that they would be tortured and killed, and would bear witness through their death, they set out to do this.
Their sufferings were no less than those of martyrdom. But they were saved because of the future things God had prepared for them:
that they should flourish as bishops. They were beaten mercilessly until their attackers thought they had died. Then they threw them like corpses
from the great height of a long flight of steps. Their limbs struck the steps as they were carried from one to another.
Each step kept casting them down onto the next, so that they were battered against them all while still alive, until they reached the ground.
They returned to their monastery rejoicing that, for God's sake, they had been found worthy to bear in their bodies the marks of Christ's sufferings.
They endured the agonies of death, as they had desired, but they did not die as martyrs, as they had expected.

They became martyrs by their own willingness, as they had longed to do. But they were not brought to completion by being killed on their own, because they were being preserved so that many might be crowned through them.
How the blessed Rabbula became bishop in the city of Edessa.
When Mar Diogenes, bishop of Edessa, died, the bishops assembled at Antioch, along with Acacius, bishop of Aleppo,
before Alexander the patriarch, to consider whom they should appoint as bishop in Edessa.
The Spirit of Jesus impressed upon their hearts that Rabbula ought to be chosen for that place, because she delighted in him.
And, as she had spoken about David, the Spirit also spoke about this man through the mouths of the priests: “I have found Rabbula my servant, who is fit for my service.
Anoint him with my holy oil by your hands. My hand will help him, and my arm will strengthen him. I will destroy before him the enemies of truth,
and I will crush those who hate him”—as indeed this prophecy was fulfilled, for he subdued the savagery of the heretics. “My faithfulness and my grace are with him,
and in my name his horn will be raised.” Thus, because of this testimony, which the Spirit of Jesus confirmed in their souls,
they sent men in haste, snatched him from his monastery, brought him to Antioch, and made him bishop.
They did not allow him, like many others, to make a show of pleading and saying, “I cannot bear and endure the burden of authority.”
Nor was he himself inclined to make a show of using these customary expressions, which people contend over when such occasions arise,
offering excuses and saying, “We will not accept, because we are not capable.” For he was a spiritual man, and he was intent on ensuring that his heart should not reproach him in anything.
He judged everything rightly in his free soul, so that no one should reproach him in anything as someone without God.
For he was afraid to resist, saying, “Perhaps I will find myself standing against God.” So he restrained himself and said:
“I never allowed myself to desire this in my mind at all, nor did the thought of it arise in my heart. I believe without any doubt that this whole affair truly comes from God,
and that he has willed that, in my weakness, I should bear the harsh yoke of authority and the weighty mystery of the priesthood. May his will be done and his good pleasure fulfilled.
For just as I obeyed his word and my soul followed him out of the evil world, so that I might keep his commandments,
so now too I accept his command in faith and, through his strength, enter the world,
solely to do his will.” Now when Edessa heard the news of the ordination of Rabbula, its shepherd,
they hurried out joyfully to meet him and welcomed him in peace. As soon as he entered and sat on the episcopal throne,
amid the many acclamations of all the people of Edessa, who honored him with their voices, he first showed his outstanding concern for the glorious arrangements of the church’s worship.
He said, “If the priests of Israel served in the tabernacle of that time with fear and reverence, how much more ought we
to serve as priests with fear and love in the church of God, which he acquired with his blood.” Through the wisdom of God within him, he also translated
the New Testament from Greek into Syriac, accurately, because of its variant readings, just as it was.
There were also many silver vessels, made for serving the clergy’s ten tables, amounting to a load in weight. He immediately ordered that they be sold,
and he justly distributed their proceeds to meet the needs of the poor. He kindly persuaded the clergy to use earthenware vessels.
He also considered selling the churches’ gold and silver vessels used in worship and giving their proceeds to the poor, saying:
“It is clear to those who understand that splendid gold and silver vessels used in worship contribute nothing extra to the honor of God.
Rather, the Spirit of God rests in pure hearts, and when these are despised, his commandment too is scorned.” But at the entreaty of many he was prevented from doing this,
because these were the offerings of their departed forefathers, which they had offered to God for the salvation of their souls.
He counseled his clergy as a father counsels his children, and admonished them as a head directs its members.
He appealed to them lovingly, saying: “You know, my brothers, that because we stand above, at the glorious height of the priesthood,
all the people who stand below us look to [?] and are guided. Therefore, let us not become a stumbling block to anyone in anything.
Let us not bring a blemish upon our ministry, so that our Lord’s ministry is dishonored through us. Let us do nothing for which we are despised by our own hearts or by other people,
and above all, never by God. Rather, in everything let us show ourselves to be servants of God, in all things worthy of God, as the apostle said.
Let us be adorned with all the fitting beauty of true righteousness. In our own persons let us offer an example of deeds, bearing witness to those who see us that our promise is true.
For this reason I ask you, by the gentleness and humility of Christ, that before everything else you keep yourselves free from the companionship of women.
Let none of you ever agree to have his brother’s daughter or his sister’s daughter live with him. And if it is possible and not burdensome for you, not even his mother or his sister, as is fitting.
to purity. Above all, do not dishonor your dignity by being served by female or male servants from the world.
Instead, let your freedom be honored by brothers who share our mysteries, as is fitting for the saints.
Or serve one another, when one of you lives with another, as Christian love requires.
Abstain completely from meat and poultry, and from bathing in bathhouses, except when compelled by illness or the distress of pain.
Do not concern yourselves with fattening the body even with ordinary foods, lest its comfort batter you with the insistence of the passions.
As for the love of money or the desire for possessions, which are foreign to our way of life, let them not even be mentioned among you.
Do not let fine clothing or elegant garments cheapen the dignity of your modesty. Instead of these things, be constant
in fasting, prayer, and the deeds of the saints. Let none of you give himself over to the world's commotion or to the lawsuits of its people.
Instead, occupy yourselves with reading the holy Scriptures. Do not love empty idleness or wander aimlessly through the city streets,
amusing yourselves with frivolous, unprofitable talk like those idle people. Instead, be diligent in the service of God's church.
By day and by night, at all times and in all your conduct, demonstrate the proof of good deeds, so that everyone may be assured by seeing you
that you believe God's promise. And as the prophet testified to them in his words, saying, “If you yield to me
and listen to me, you will not only eat the richness of the earth, but also inherit the blessedness of heaven. But if you refuse to yield and are contentious,
here you will be despised by us in everyone's sight, and you will be condemned to the punishment of hell before the angels and in the sight of all the worlds.”
For those whom his love did not persuade gently, fear of him subjected by force.
For he justly struck down the proud among them so that they would repent, and discerningly honored the humble among them so that they would be comforted.
And those who behaved contemptuously and exalted themselves above their companions because of their wealth,
he greatly abased and humbled so that they would feel it. But those who, amid suffering chosen voluntarily or imposed by poverty, conducted their lives humbly and with complete uprightness,
he raised up, honored, and loved, entrusting them with leadership of the church. And he took care that those who were chosen through him for the ranks of the priesthood
were accomplished in these and many more virtues besides. For he spent a long time taking pains over this concern,
so that through his investigation he could gain reliable assurance about trustworthy men whom he might bring forward for the service of Christ.
For, such was the strength of his resolve, it was easier for him courageously to offer his right hand to be cut off without mercy
than to stretch it out rashly over the head of someone about whom he had received no truthful testimony. For he fulfilled the apostle's words in practice,
and would never consent to lay his hand hastily on anyone, lest he share in other people's sins.
Instead, he would bring forward, by the laying on of his hand, someone who was free even from the passions of his own soul and body.
to the holy mysteries of the priesthood. For he would loudly proclaim before the whole church the names of all those whom he wished to admit to the clergy.
He solemnly charged all his hearers by the word of God to disclose anything they knew about these men that was contrary to God.
Besides this, he would also investigate them privately through every kind of inquiry, also ascertaining from the men themselves whether [?] they were deficient in anything.
For he earnestly took every care that, like the choice sacrifice and acceptable offering of Abel, the first priest,
people without blemish should be offered to God through his hands. For his concern was that, as far as human nature allows,
priests should resemble the angels of heaven in their ministry. As for his constant admonitions to the chaste community of consecrated men,
who can recount them? For throughout all the years of his life that he spent in the priesthood—twenty-four years—
he never ceased this exhortation. We cannot record and commit to writing the great care expressed in his admonitions every single day.
For he solemnly warned them, with threats as well, to keep entirely away from association with women.
He commanded and admonished them not to eat meat or bathe while they were healthy. And not to become entangled in worldly business,
he advised and urged them. He also laid down that they must not lend money at interest or for a fixed profit.
With his gracious words he encouraged them to love one another. He advised them that, if possible, each of them should live
with a companion. He exhorted them and asked them to devote themselves to fasting and persevere in prayer.
He urged them to show in everything, by their deeds and words, that they were disciples of Christ.

In his teaching he also gave instructions about clothing, footwear, and the cutting of their hair, so that they would not appear immodest. He also constantly admonished the whole community of consecrated women,
that the face of Christ's bride should never be seen by anyone in the street without the covering of modesty.
They were never to display any sign of immodesty in any aspect of their appearance. And none of them, without the company of several others, should go to a gathering or a house of mourning
under any circumstances. He wanted all the daughters of each deaconess to live with her in watchfulness, holiness, and chastity.
For, he said, the unity of many women can safeguard them all. He strove by every means
to lead people away from sin and bring them into fellowship with righteousness. For like a diligent shepherd who tends his flocks with care,
such was the care of this spiritual shepherd for the rational flock entrusted to him by God.
For he was afraid to neglect his care for it even a little, lest, through concern for himself alone, a single soul from his people should perish and he suffer loss.
For he was always keeping watch with great vigilance, praying for the flock and wearing himself out with concern for it,
so that there should be nothing evil in it, either secretly or openly. For in his love he was willing, if possible, that
his flock should do good, even if he himself were despised, in keeping with his goodwill toward it.
For he constantly labored on her behalf with great anguish in prayer to God, while in the rich pastures of the Holy Scriptures
he nourished her with their spiritual sayings. With his living words he diligently gave her divine teaching to drink, as though from a sweet stream.
He guarded the well-fed sheep with his warnings, healed the sick with his consolations, and strengthened the weak with his encouragements,
so that none of his flock would ever stray through neglect on his part. For his soul trusted in the blessed hope reserved as the reward for his labor,
according to God's testimony, when he addressed him in the person of the man with the talents: “Good and faithful servant! You have been faithful over a little; I will put you in charge of much.
Enter into your master's joy.” As for his excellent instructions to the village priests, the monks, and the members of the covenant, there is much to tell.
As far as we can, we are recording some of these instructions addressed to them. For by God's grace his speech was always seasoned as though with salt,
and it could impart grace to those who received it faithfully. For his words were credible to his hearers because they saw his deeds.
For his actions and his words benefited everyone who heard and saw them, and everyone accepted them as reliable witnesses.
His speech was awe-inspiring in its plainness, weighty in its correction, endearing in its exhortation, and beneficial in practice to its hearers. From
the abundance of his heart, indeed, his lips spoke, and they urged everyone toward the purity of his deeds.
For he was not willing to entertain with his speech, but only to show how a person might turn toward God, from evil deeds to deeds of righteousness.
It was not because his knowledge of these and similar things was deficient,
but because he concerned himself only with things that were excellent and beneficial to people. For he never undertook to use the ornament of polished words in his preaching.
For he did not speak in church to display the superiority of his wisdom and win praise for himself, like others who are despised by their hearers.
Rather, he took care to cut his hearers' hearts away from evil toward good with his piercing speech. He was deeply concerned that they should not withhold God's praise within themselves.
As though he had clothed himself in the mighty voice of Jeremiah the prophet in his preaching, he cried out like a trumpet in the people's ears,
urging them to abstain from the wickedness and sins produced by laxity. He also rebuked those who, to the shameful and scandalous entertainment held in the theater and the circus,
hurried eagerly to watch. But the disgraceful spectacle of fanged beasts spilling human blood in the stadium
he abolished entirely by his authoritative command, making righteous threats and saying, “Far be it that this should happen in a city of believers:
that people who in their faith eat God's body and drink his blood should watch human flesh being devoured
wickedly by savage beasts for entertainment.” Through his words he showed them the wounds of sin
that, without their noticing, were taking hold of their souls under the guise of amusement. It was as though he himself, because of his love for them, was being wounded in their place.
Such was his genuine anguish over those who, through their disobedience, were doing worse and worse things to the destruction of their lives.
For he did not hesitate to admonish the people to turn from their evil deeds.
He used to speak as though he could clear himself merely by giving warning. But so that what God had promised through the prophet might be fulfilled in him:
“If you bring out what is precious from what is worthless, you will be like my mouth.” This was how he labored with all his strength.
As for those who, after pledging themselves to virginity and holiness, were being struck in their bodies by the wounds of sins,
he alone could tell us in his own words what pangs of sorrow in his heart were piercing his soul on their account. Or who among those whose upright conduct was sound
would he hear had become sick through some evil deed, without himself becoming sick with grief over that person?
Or which of Christ’s disciples would he receive news of, that he had fallen away from his commitment or stumbled in his faith,
without himself burning as though in fire with pain on that person’s behalf? For at all times, like a skilled physician,
he knew how to respond to the changing symptoms of the diseases of souls. Sometimes, with compassionate discipline suited to checking
wickedness, he would cut away the corruption of the ulcer as though with sharp iron, so that the patient might suffer and live.

Sometimes, with rebukes in words that he knew how to apply to the source of folly, he would treat the severity of the disease as though with powerful medicinal roots, so that the patient might repent and benefit.
At other times, with the peaceful persuasion of his gentle words, suited to correcting the offender, he would treat the sickness of the passion as though with soothing medicines,
so that he might [?] and be built up. For in every approach his concern was this alone: that they should come to the health of repentance that turns the soul toward life,
by taking up the burden of his teaching. In these ways, then, and in many more besides, he continually showed his concern for his flock.
For he truly feared the just sentence pronounced in God’s warning against those shepherds who neglect their flock while taking care of themselves.
And as someone who truly believed in the strict accounting that would finally be held with the shepherds, according to the word of our Lord that testifies to them,
“From anyone entrusted with much, much will also be demanded,” his heart was zealous with all his strength
to admonish, teach, and correct everyone in every commandment, whether by word or deed, in season and out of season,
although his natural strength was unequal to the readiness of his will. For his good will was stronger than his natural strength, and the consciences of the upright bear witness to this.
The personal virtuous deeds of Mar Rabbula the bishop consisted in these constant practices.
He always labored with discernment in frequent fasting, and even his eating served to complete his fast.
For not only did he give himself no room for laxity by eating varied foods, but even at mealtimes he never consented to eat enough to satisfy his hunger.
With three ounces of bread and one plain cooked dish, he would ease the tightness in his stomach, while abstaining from oil and wine.
For from the day when the name of Christ was invoked over him, he was never willing to consent to satisfy his hunger with anything.
Through his endurance he waged constant war against everything desirable, and he was never overcome so as to crave and taste even something insignificant.
Rather, in his victory he always stood high and far above these weakening passions, which bring mighty men low under the harsh bondage of dependence on them.
For he taught everyone by his own example a humbling fast, free from boasting, and moderation in food.
As for the lavish offerings of different foods that many people faithfully brought him for his own use, whenever he was persuaded to accept them,
he would send them to the sick and infirm in the hospice, and to those suffering from illnesses in the secluded life of solitude.
The humble equipment of his modest table consisted entirely of these things: a glass bowl, an earthenware jug, and a wooden spoon.
He also trained the members of his household in these same practices, according to their ability, so that they might embody the pattern of his virtue in themselves.
They too were eager to do this of their own free will. For they spent most of the night with him in continual vigils of psalms and prayers,
while throughout the days they labored over the affairs of the oppressed and over reading in his presence.
They fasted with him every day, and their needs were met by two dishes, one of grain and one of vegetables.
The pallor that marked him was enough to adorn their faces too, along with his,
so that its appearance revealed their austere way of life. For they looked like people who shared a single [?] table.
Their faces were thus tinged with a jaundiced appearance. For even during his episcopate he was eager to double the hard labors of his monastic life.
For the spiritual gift of the priesthood became his helper and companion in every good work. This too is remarkable:
of the men who lived with him for twenty-four years, not one was able to bring him under the yoke of that long stretch of time,
so as to enter his presence casually through habitual familiarity, or to speak freely with him.
Instead, every day their fear of him increased, and just as though they were only beginning to enter his presence for the first time, so
their minds trembled in awe of him. Yet they were not frightened of him as of someone harsh and terrifying,
but held themselves back as before someone discerning and dignified. For not only was his freedom never compromised in their eyes by anything contemptible,
but he never willingly gave them cause to murmur against him even in their consciences. For if he himself was not conscious of anything hateful within himself,
how much more radiant and dignified he was in their sight and in everyone else's! He inspired fear while also being loved. These members of his household, together with all his clergy,
were continually bound by him through the word of God not to accept anything at all from anyone as a gift or a mark of honor.
He also continually placed all the priests under his authority under threat of the penalty of suspension,
so that people did not dare bring anything at all to anyone in his household or to any of the clergy.
“If,” he said, “they bring a gift in the name of a blessing, then we, who are held in greater honor than they, ought to give. And if this is an honor offered ceremonially,
it is fitting that we, who have authority, should bestow honor. But if it is a gift exacted by compulsion, then we, who are better provided for than they, ought to make provision.
In every case, then, it is we who are obliged to give, not to receive.” For the greater part of his episcopate,
Who among the monks could compare with him? For he mourned inwardly, and his constant clothing was a hair shirt and a modest cloak.
At the time of the church service, he wore the one winter cloak he owned in winter, and a single cape in summer. The bedding
of his humble bed consisted only of these things: a bed covering and a [?],
and a small pillow cut from [?] sufficed beneath his head. As for his practice of prayer before God,
the appointed times of worship were not enough for him. Therefore, from time to time he set aside a week of days for continual prayer.
He confined himself within his dwelling, away from human company, hiding himself from the sight of those who shared his quarters. He even ceased reading,
so that, free from human voices and noise, in the peaceful stillness of his thoughts, his mind might be wholly gathered toward God,
his thoughts awakened by remembrance of his Lord, and his understanding set aflame by the Spirit of his God, and so that his prayer might benefit him in his solitude.
Thus he might offer his Lord, in the temple of his hidden inner life, an acceptable sacrifice of pure supplication, carrying in the hands of his mind
the remembrance of the sins of the world, to receive from him forgiveness of their sins through his boundless mercy.
In this stolen solitude of his few days of prayer, who could know how to recount the wonderful changes that the Spirit of God brought about in his mind,
except those who were perfect like him and had been trained in the hidden mysteries of prayer?
Perhaps it was easy for these people to discern, from the meaning of its words, the hidden signs that God's grace was working in his heart.
And since those who feed on divine love truly hunger for it again, and those who drink it thirst for it again, he was all the more compelled by the good desire of love for
his Lord to leave the city and the pressures of its affairs for forty days each year,
and eagerly fly far away and settle in his monastery in the wilderness of Chalcis. There he would plead in prayer and cry out mightily for his requests to be answered.
Whenever he stood before God in prayer at the head of the people, for as long as he stood there from early morning, his eyes never ceased their sorrowful weeping.
The abundant flow of his tears was enough to move even hardened and merciless people at the sight of it:
how, from the fervor of his spirit, they streamed down from his eyes onto his breast as he sat on the throne during worship.
For he ministered as a priest before God with discernment, in reverent fear, as our human nature ought, and in the confidence of true love, as God wills.
Through these heavenly ways of life, which were visible in this angel in the flesh,
many different gifts of healing were distributed to the sick through the power of his prayer.
His faith drove away from people the grievous afflictions caused by evil spirits. His word, too, was proved
in practice to all who knew him: when he was justly angry with someone or showed favor with discernment, God acted with him.
Because of this awe, the mere mention of his prayer was enough even to settle a quarrel between one man and another peacefully.
Often, indeed, the people, in the fervor of their faith in him, would willingly tear his clothes and pass them among themselves from one person to another as a blessing,
so that a blessing from his garments would be brought to many of them.
Many inhabitants of the city and of his entire jurisdiction would even give their sons and daughters the honored name of Rabbula, in faith, as a blessing.
For his flock sought shelter beneath the wings of his name and his prayers. They prayed for his perfect health and that his life might be prolonged for many years.
For he was a strong wall firmly surrounding his entire territory, one that had never, on any occasion, been overcome by the enemy’s cunning.
Those who lived within the fortress of his boundaries conducted their lives in an orderly way, in peaceful quiet, through their trust in him.
For he used his authority to restrain everyone from plunder, oppression, or merciless demands. For who would dare to plunder a wretched person,
or oppress a poor person, or harass his neighbor, without God’s justice being revealed against him through Rabbula’s zeal, to discipline him?
For a rich man who mistreated a poor person would be frightened and checked by the mere mention of him.
A man who cheated someone of lower standing in settling accounts would shrink back in fear and tremble at his name.
For everyone would settle his dealings with his neighbor beforehand with an honest mind, so that he would not be put to shame in judgment before him.
For the greedy mouths of oppressive people were bound by the bridle of his justice, so that the injustice of their oppression would not openly assail the lowly.
The grasping hands of plunderers were bound with the cords of his uprightness,

so that the force of their strength would not defraud the weak. For who among the leading men of his city, or among those who sought protection in the honored households of rulers in order to do wrong,
ever raised his head and snorted arrogantly without immediately being crushed by his pursuing truth, so that he regretted his insolence?
Or which of the judges [?] who lived in his days thought [?] against his word, and was not swiftly [?] God overtook him with the infliction of [?] to suffer for the wrong he had done.
Or who [?] all those in authority [?] exalted himself above his humility [?], and was not speedily [?] the justice of God, so that he would repent of his sin.
For all the orphans and widows in his territory lived as though in a peaceful harbor through their hope in him,
so that, sheltered by him, they were not violently harmed by the battering waves of accursed plunderers. For in his days,

men serving in the army were restrained by fear of him not only from cheating an artisan or harassing villagers; even to honor the Christian garb in whoever wore it, however contemptible he might appear,
they were forcibly compelled by his own dignity. For God had so caused fear and love of him to rest upon everyone, each in his own rank,
that many, through fear and shame, were kept from numerous sins because of him.
It was difficult [?] for anyone to be found in his territory [?] the world, who would contemptuously disrupt the order of marriage [?].
But [?] one man, two sisters [?], while he had children [?] the first, who had died, he did not [?].
He would never allow anyone to marry his brother’s daughter or his sister’s daughter. Still less would he allow a man to leave his wife on any pretext.
This could not happen at all while he was aware of it, for he would not allow anything to be done contrary to God’s will.
that was reported to him. Often, however, even the mere recollection of the formidable power of his godly zeal was enough
to check beforehand, in many people, the vile impulse toward impending evils, so that they would not be committed.
For which of the foolish would have dared, in his days, openly and shamelessly to raise his eyes to gaze at the beautiful face of a chaste woman?
For merely remembering the holiness of this devout man would make the earth beneath him and the heavens above him tremble,
and his body would be startled by it and grow quiet in gentle relief. Or which of those being trained as disciples of Christ
would wear patterned and perfumed clothes, to make an impressive appearance in them, parading proudly through the city streets,
without feeling ashamed of himself and rejecting his desire, when he saw with what humble bearing this dignified man stood at the head of the people?
Or which of the gluttons, enslaved to the evil mastery of their appetite, would remember the table of this pure man,
whose hunger was never satisfied, and dare to eat greedily or drink excessively? For some, fear of him
kept them in order, while admiration for him restrained others. Again, which of the lovers of money, who were wasting their lives in the futility of accumulating it,
would carefully consider this steward of God, and where grace obtained those seven thousand gold coins in a single year,
which it distributed through his hands to the poor, apart from the expenses of his ministers and all the schools in his city,
without immediately judging himself, condemning himself, hating his fault, and hastening to share in the giving of alms, following the example of this righteous man,
who imitated God’s mercy in everything? Throughout all the years of his life, he could not be persuaded to build anything on earth,
except only half of the northern wall of the church building in his city, because the seriousness of the damage to it compelled him.
He repaired it in a few days. He used to say, “It is we who live on what belongs to the poor, according to a just judgment,
not they who are supported by what belongs to us, according to God’s justice. For it was for the support of orphans, widows, and the needy
that the church inherited from believers the property it possesses. As for us who administer it, we are permitted to use it simply to meet our bodily needs,
just like the rest of the poor, according to a just judgment, and not according to the will of our body, which desires what harms our spirit.”
Much could be said about the keenness of his knowledge and the clarity of his understanding: how he perceived each person’s actions from that person’s words, because with the Spirit of God
he was filled. Falsehoods that stole the appearance of truth could not lead him astray through lies.
For the spirit of God’s wisdom within him so thoroughly confounded the understanding of those pleading their cases before him that, when their speech became entangled through fear,
they would speak the truth with their own mouths against their will. What further witness did he need for the conviction of the accused?
It was enough for him to discern for himself, through his examination, who was guilty and who was innocent.
so that judgment would issue from him not perversely but justly. For, as though people’s thoughts were moving through his mind,
he would probe their secrets in his investigation to discover the truth. For wisdom, understanding, and very great breadth of mind
had been given him by God, as to Solomon. There was no limit to the measure of his justice, so powerfully did it assert itself against contemptuous people
who used their strength to wrong the lowly in their arrogance. Nor was there any measure to the wealth of his kindness,
so richly was it poured out upon those poor in body and spirit, who through their endurance had distinguished themselves in the furnace of poverty.
For in his justice and compassion he conducted himself in everything according to God’s will alone. He too was another Moses in his generation and his time,
whose righteous zeal was detested and hated by wrongdoers, and whose discerning humility was despised and scorned by the arrogant. Yet it was not
in these things alone that he resembled Moses; rather, he resembled him in everything. In his difficult struggles against a multitude of religious cults,
he resembled Joshua son of Nun, and especially Josiah in his zeal. For his Lord also said to him, as to Joshua,
“Be strong and courageous, and do not be afraid, because I am with you to help you.”
For just as Joshua son of Nun and Josiah had found the land of Canaan overgrown with every kind of forest of paganism,
so he too found the whole territory of Edessa thickly overgrown with every kind of forest of sin. For there in Edessa, especially, there flourished
the evil teaching of Bardaisan, until he condemned and defeated it. For that accursed Bardaisan had previously, through his cunning
and the sweetness of his songs, won over all the leading men of the city to his side, so that he might shelter behind them as behind strong walls.
For the fool, going astray himself and leading his followers astray, imagined that through the failing strength of his supporters he could establish his error securely.
But this wise farmer of the fields of the heart did not merely strive to remove the choking weeds from his land and leave the wheat growing—for that was easy.
Rather, in his wisdom he worked to change the weeds themselves into wheat. For this was indeed the difficult task.
So, instead of the terrifying sound of the trumpets of Joshua and his companions, who shouted against the walls of Jericho and brought them crashing down—
and he slaughtered the people and devoted their possessions to the Lord—this victorious commander of Jesus Christ, with a peaceful
and loving voice, was able through the power of his God to demolish their synagogue quietly and carry all its treasure into his church.
He even took its stones for use. But as for the people themselves, on whom all his care was focused,
he persuaded them kindly, brought them into obedience gently, and turned them to the sure truth of the apostolic Church, while they renounced and anathematized their error.
Then he baptized them into Christ and admitted them to his worship. In this way, through his teaching, he overcame a multitude of religious cults
and subjected them to the truth. Throughout all the years of his priesthood, he baptized thousands of Jews and tens of thousands of heretics into Christ.
Again, with the same armor of the Spirit in which he was clothed, he was able to bring even the Arians into obedience to the truth of the exalted Trinity.
For he demolished their house of prayer, brought them close to himself, and gathered the people who were with them into his flock.
As we together give equal glory to the one nature in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
As for the followers of Marcion, I cannot show, even at great length, how great his concern for them was.
Thus this great physician, distinguished in every way, through his diligence healed this putrid, cancerous sore of the Marcionites’ error, with the help of his God and through his patience with them.
For God instilled in them a fear of the holy Rabbula, and they faithfully accepted his truth, renouncing their error.
Likewise, through his divine wisdom, he also brought the crazed Manichaeans to a settled mind and discerning knowledge. They confessed
therefore, as he wished, and believed in the truth, were baptized into Christ, and were added to his people. As for the disgraceful error and unclean tradition of the Borborites,
wherever he could, he confined them to monasteries for the rest of their lives, with great compassion. For their folly is great,
and their filthy teaching is repulsive for pure lips to speak into clean ears. For this reason he also laid down a restriction for them:
they were never to be found in his jurisdiction. As for the heretical Audians and Sadducees, who separated themselves from communion with the church, as people cut off from the truth,
and produced for themselves a false priesthood in the likeness of the true one, wandering after fabricated revelations and blind to the truth,
this true shepherd, who took such care of his flock, dealt with them in the following ways. He scattered their congregation and made them strangers to the sanctuary they had adorned.
He expelled them from it and settled in their place brothers who shared our sacred mysteries. Those among them who repented he admitted into his flock.
In the same way he also showed his concern for the heretical Messalians. He brought these close to himself and persuaded them in Christ.
They accepted gladly, renouncing their error. This true shepherd also strove to imitate the compassion of the Father in heaven.
In keeping with his perfect love for God, he demonstrated through his deeds an equal care for the good and the wicked.
For this reason he did not neglect even the wayward people of the children of Israel. Rather, at all times his excellent care

for them was evident in his actions. For not only did he not deprive them of a share in his generous almsgiving, but many of them were also persuaded to receive the life-giving seal of Christ’s baptism
gladly each year, through his constant exhortation to them.
But after the blessed Rabbula had broken the arrows and bows of those who hated the truth with the shield of his faith,
and had defeated the enemy of truth with the armor of God that he bore, and had beaten down all the shoots of error by trampling them with his truth,
and had wiped away the repulsive sores of the unbelievers’ blasphemies with the medicine of his teaching, and had made his entire flock one sound body, a mature human being,
he was now close to enjoying a little peace and resting upon the gains he had carried off in his battles against false teachings.
He went on to concern himself only with himself and the household of his faith, in matters of greater perfection.
He warned, exhorted, and urged them, saying, “We must gain heavenly riches through works of righteousness while we are in the world.”
that he himself might prove a true guide for us toward a good end, and that through him we might confidently reach the kingdom of God. While, then, he was exhorting and guiding with these words,

and was encouraging others in many similar ways through deeds and words, there was a certain bitter root whose youthful shoots, as trustworthy people who knew him say, were consumed by the fire of lust,
until he grew old and worn out and was destroyed by death, and his pampered body rotted and became dung in the earth. From this man, then,
the spirit of falsehood brought forth a certain accursed shoot: Nestorius, the evil disciple of this Theodore.
And he put deadly fruits into his mouth, poisoned with hidden death. This man, then, had already received the accursed seed from that man's teaching and from his association with him.
But because he was cowed by fear of people, it lay stifled and hidden in the soil of his evil heart.
But when, by one pretext or another, he seized for himself the exalted episcopal throne in the great imperial city,
the fool, deceived by his own pride, imagined that through the harsh force of authority and with the help of the empire's high officials,
he could easily turn everyone to his blasphemy. From then on he grew bold enough to speak unjustly against the Most High and to bring abuse upon the woman who bore him.
But I tremble even to recall the blasphemies of the man who dared to say, “Blessed Mary is not the Mother of God, but the mother of a human being.”
“For,” he said, “if Mary is the mother of the Son, then Elizabeth is also the mother of the Holy Spirit.”
In the contemptuousness of his embittered heart, he did not tremble or even feel ashamed before the apostle's statement: “God sent his Son, and he came to be from a woman,
and came to be under the law.” Instead, he stubbornly persisted in his arrogance, granting the Son only an indwelling in Jesus, like that of the Spirit in John.
And again he said, “That servant who was born of a woman himself suffered, according to his nature, the things that befell him.
And the Son who dwelt in him performed whatever signs he wished.” But rather than continue recounting that accursed man's error, these statements are enough to make known
to discerning people the greatness of his wickedness. For he was so reckless with his own life that he dared, through the distinctions in his words, to present two different sons:
one by nature and one by grace. When these blasphemies spoken by the rebel reached the ears of this holy man, his heart groaned with fear, and he was shaken.
For through God's wisdom within him, he had already perceived what terrible harm would swiftly come upon Christ's flock through that shameful intruder.
From then on he continued speaking against that man's error, substantiating his own words
from the reliable testimony of the divine Scriptures, declaring that holy Mary is truly the Mother of God.
“For look,” he said, “the prophet Isaiah cries out: ‘The virgin will conceive and bear a son, and they will call his name Immanuel,’
which means ‘Our God is with us.’ And look, Jeremiah proclaims: ‘Our God appeared on earth and lived among human beings.’
And look, the apostle Paul confirms the prophets' words and makes known his Lord's birth in the flesh from the descendants of the house of David,
and that he was revealed to be the Son of God. And look, John explains in his Gospel
that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. ‘And we saw his glory,’ he says, ‘glory as of the only Son from the Father.’ For he himself had said:
In the beginning was the Word. And the Word became flesh, without his nature being changed—God forbid! Rather, he who is Lord of all took the form of a servant.
For he became a complete human being without ceasing to be God. Rather, the unity of his divinity and his humanity is preserved, and there is one nature
and person of the eternal Son, just as he was even before he became incarnate.
For in this way he also willingly suffered in the flesh, although by nature he cannot suffer. Therefore he died in the body and was alive in the spirit.
And he proclaimed good news to the souls held captive in Sheol. Then he rose in the glory of his Father and ascended to heaven, where he had been from eternity and remains forever.
These, then, were the spiritual arrows that our blessed father drew and shot from the bow of his faith, using the taut string of his truthful tongue.
Although they passed painlessly into the people's ears and built them up, they struck the heart of his opponent to cause him pain and bring him to repentance.
At that very time, a good opportunity arose for him to enter there as well, and he openly exposed the ancient error of the new Jew.
While this rejected silver was still gilded with the priesthood, and while he was still puffed up with arrogant pride,
and sitting on the lofty throne of authority, face to face before the whole assembled church, he proclaimed the word of truth rightly, in a loud voice and without concealment.
He corrected the crookedness of that man's false teaching through the true confession of his own faith.
At the request of many and for everyone's benefit, we also intend to write down, after our account of him,
the discourse that the blessed man delivered in the tyrant's hearing in the Great Church of Constantinople, so that everyone may clearly see and believe
how great was the boldness with which he spoke with authority, through the powerful testimony of his
pure conscience. Nor did he neglect to expose that man's error and make his own truth known also to the faithful, Christ-loving emperors,
and to all the emperor's high officials who held authority. As though he were one of God's angels and a successor of the apostles,
they received him with reverence and love and with great honor. And because of their fervent love for him,
they eagerly pressed forward in affection and faith to kiss his hands, so that they might receive his blessing and be enriched.
For the good reputation of his godly virtue encouraged them to do good works even from a distance. Thus, on many occasions,
they, and people much farther away than they were in the upper Roman Empire, sent him many thousands in gold to provide for the poor.
How much more, then, did close association with him, seeing him so full of benefits, and his delightful conversation with them
encourage them toward every good thing through his exhortation! Yet this man, who had gladly accepted the gold sent to him from afar,
when the emperors and dignitaries themselves offered him much gold, together with jewelry and clothing, and asked him to accept their offering,
was apprehensive, saying, “Although the circumstances that compelled me to come up here are quite clear,
they might think that I sought a borrowed guise in which to appear before them and receive a gift from them.”

But because he was not despised in any way by any one of them, and did not surrender his freedom at all, he was all the more honored and trusted in their eyes. Thus, through these things that we have already
mentioned, he rebuked Nestorius, exposed his error, warned the people against him, and made known his own true faith.
He also persuaded the emperors and enlightened them with his truth. He built up the high officials and strengthened them through his teaching, and gave abundant help in words and deeds
to everyone who saw him in the cities through which he passed on his journey there and back, until, through mercy, he reached his own city. He himself continued,
still fighting constantly against that newly arisen impiety, until that good shepherd who suffered for his flock rose against it in righteous judgment,
through the faithful and holy bishops of the south and the west, who, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit,
passed sentence and cast him out of the priestly rank. He is being kept for God's righteous judgment, at which he will give an account together with those who agree with him.
But since I cannot set out in a lengthy account our father's battle against this error,
or, again, describe in a few words the blessed man's struggle for the true faith of the church,
the forty-six letters that he wrote to priests, emperors, high officials, and monks are sufficient. If grace helps us,
we will labor to translate them from Greek into Syriac, so that they themselves may make known to those who read them
how his divine zeal burned and blazed as though in fire. For in his hope and love he shared Paul's faith.

For although he did not pray, like the apostle, to be cut off from Christ for his brothers and relatives according to the flesh, nevertheless, to be sacrificed for Jesus for his brothers and relatives

in the Spirit, ten thousand times if that were possible, was his earnest desire. And since circumstances did not allow him to do this openly, through the suffering he willingly accepted and the afflictions he freely chose and displayed in his own person,
through the constant sufferings of the cross, he passed the days of his life apart from this world.
But he imitated Paul not only in these things. He also concerned himself with the great gift entrusted to Paul by the apostles who preceded him: caring for the poor.
He took care to do this himself as well. As though he himself, together with Paul, had received this command from the apostles to care for the poor, so diligently did he observe it.
For who can recount the great care he took to provide for the poor, and especially the surpassing love he had for the holy poor?
For in each of the secluded dwellings among the monasteries of the devout men who had lived uprightly in seclusion—
those whose bones, even after their departure, became a sweet fragrance in Christ—they would prepare a separate cell for him at his word, as he wished,
so that whenever he went to visit them, to be helped in his faith by those who had fallen asleep in peace, and especially to help their sons through his exhortation,
he could stay there alone in silence, persevering in prayer acceptable to God and benefiting from his prayer.
Thus, while the offerings of his almsgiving were many and were bestowed abundantly on everyone at all times,
he also longed to offer himself deliberately as a sacrifice to Christ on behalf of everyone. And in keeping with the desire
of his goodwill toward God and toward everyone, he nourished the poor, his fellow servants, from what belonged to his Lord, for as long as he lived in the world, according to God's will.
Even after his death, he left them the good inheritance of prayer and entrusted them to the grace of God, the mother of all,
so that from it they might receive provision each day for their needs. For the fire of love for him remains alive and is preserved in their hearts.
The cherished remembrance of Rabbula’s beloved name also feeds and kindles the fire of love for him in their hearts.
Therefore all those in need trade upon his good name as though it were valuable merchandise, to meet the needs of their distress.
For as soon as those who love him hear Rabbula’s cherished name, love for him is kindled in their hearts.
Their compassion wells up, and they give alms. The recipient rejoices, the giver benefits, and God is glorified.
And the service of our father Rabbula is also kept in remembrance before his Lord on account of this, in accordance with what is said among the faithful:
“Blessed is the servant through whom his master’s name is praised.” From the love of the poor that he possessed in his soul,
he made an excellent improvement in his city’s hospital, which previously had existed in name alone,
and not in practice—an improvement truly worthy of God’s praise and rightly deserving of praise for him.
For he assigned it certain villages from his church’s property, so that its expenses would be met from their revenues.
The way was also opened for many people to bequeath property and possessions to it, so that its revenue amounted to as much as a thousand dinars in a single
year. From these revenues, comfort was provided for the sick and assistance for the healthy, under the arrangements he prescribed.
For who among those whose conscience was corrupt would not have longed to feed on the various dishes

that were prepared for the sick through the care required by his command? Indeed, it was impossible for anyone to tell from an offensive smell that sick people and people afflicted with sores lay there,
because of the care and cleanliness maintained for them at his command. Their beds were inviting, with soft bedding spread upon them.
Dirty or shabby articles were never seen either in their beds or upon them. For their comfortable care and the provision of their necessities,
he had placed faithful deacons, genuinely devoted to their welfare, in charge of these things, together with chaste brothers full of love,
who were to do no other work besides caring for them. He also did the same for the women’s hospital, which had not existed at all,
but was quickly established at his command, using stones from four temples of idols that had been demolished in his city by his authoritative order.
There, outside the city, he prudently appointed a capable deaconess, together with women of the covenant,
so that they might modestly and readily carry out the service needed for the women’s comfort. Moreover, through his love for God, directed compassionately toward his fellow human beings,
he burned and blazed as though with fire. He showed his great concern especially for the afflicted poor,
who lived apart outside the city as hated and rejected people.
For he appointed a trustworthy deacon over them, who lived beside them with upright brothers assigned to their care.
Everything they needed was continually supplied from the inner church. He himself also, at all times,
comforted their souls in deed and word. Through the practical exercise of his generosity, he relieved the suffering caused by their ailments.
With the word of God he encouraged their minds, so that they would not be overwhelmed by sorrow. And many times, to comfort their souls,
he gave them the greeting of a holy kiss on their foul lips, these people whose bodies were wasting away. And so that they would not lose heart under God's discipline
toward them, he strengthened them. He urged them to give thanks to our Lord all the more because of their afflictions, saying,
“Remember, my brothers, that it is written that Lazarus, because he endured suffering, was considered worthy to rest in Abraham's bosom, in the place of the kingdom.”
Through all these things, and the many things we have mentioned before, and the rest that we cannot recount, his priesthood
—true, and belonging to this man of illustrious name—was shining forth. The wicked and the insolent trembled before his justice,
and the weak and the poor were supported by his generosity. He graciously inclined his ear to those who had been wronged,
and in his zeal he was an advocate for the oppressed. By his word and deed he encouraged those who did good.
He always gave the humble a helping hand to raise them up. In his own person he embodied the deeds required by the law
and wrapped his Lord's commandment around himself like a garment. Examples of his God's mercy could be seen in him, and he poured it out abundantly to the boundaries [?] of his jurisdiction.
All the families of the region of Edessa boasted and took pride in him, while he boasted in his Lord and drew strength from him.
He saw God's acts of deliverance plainly before his eyes, and he placed no confidence at all in his own righteousness.
After all these things, it happened, as it commonly did, that he was stricken with bodily illness, on the first day of July,
when he had completed twenty-four years and three months of his life as bishop. Let us also consider and gain insight from this miraculous sign that occurred in his case:
although the man had suffered from various illnesses all his days, on the day when this final illness pressed upon him,
it was immediately revealed to him, and he said openly to those close to him, “The time of my rest has come upon me.” He also showed it by his actions,

like someone to whom it had truly been whispered by the Spirit that the end of his life was approaching. This was evident from the charitable aid that he was accustomed to distribute every month of Kanun:
he hurried to arrange its distribution promptly in July. He immediately sent his alms through his attendants
to the north and the east, where he was accustomed to give. He sent others carrying his gifts to the monasteries in the west and the south,
whose inhabitants lived in hope of God's grace, extending his gifts even to the holy poor who lived in the wilderness of Jerusalem,
just as it is written that blessed Paul also collected charitable aid for them. Others went out
to the territory of all the cities under his authority. Others distributed gifts to the priests and to the communities of consecrated men and women under his authority.
He gave to the ascetics and monks within his jurisdiction, and provided for the poor in the villages throughout the entire region of Edessa.
Meanwhile, others in his city were again distributing to all the needy, to the monks, and to the men and women of the covenant.
He also provided for widows and the afflicted as he wished. He added many books to these gifts, and forgave all the debts he had inherited.
He tore up the documents for the large sums of gold he had lent to craftsmen. With his own hand he gave a gift equally to all the clergy.
After he had fulfilled every good intention and accomplished every noble desire, and saw that he had rebelled against the world and its hindrances and despised the Evil One and his enticements,
and had also scorned the body and its inducements, he raised his voice confidently, supported by the good testimony of his virtuous deeds,
boasting in the Lord, as the illustrious Paul said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished my race, and I have kept my faith.
From now on, the crown of righteousness is reserved for me, which my Lord, the righteous judge, will award me on that day. Into his hand I commit my spirit.”
He said these things as he prayed fervently at the time of his death. He marked his face with the cross and lovingly blessed those standing before him.
He joyfully surrendered his soul to his Lord. On the seventh day of the month of Ab, the news of his death suddenly spread through his city.
Perhaps even its walls trembled, and its inhabitants were shaken by the sound of the anguished cry
of its residents. In their sorrowful wailing, each person's voice joined the next, continuing without interruption.
For the whole city became a single chorus of mourners, divided into eighteen groups of deaconesses
inside the church courtyards, with the Jewish chorus of mourners outside. The whole city wept for him, in the streets, in the courtyards, and inside the church,
with mournful laments that brought forth bitter sighs and sorrowful tears: the priests with all the members of the covenant, and the laity with the Jews.
They bewailed their own plight, saying, “Alas for every one of us, without exception! What a lover of God and lover of humanity we have been deprived of!
What a true shepherd and leader in righteousness we have lost, becoming orphans! From what a provider of good things, who bore the burden of fellowship, we have been separated!
From what a scribe of the truth, upright in his faith, we have been parted! Of what a counselor in good things
and encourager of virtue we have been bereft! For who,” they said, “will succeed this compassionate physician for us in his deeds?
The sufferings of his fellow human beings were imprinted on his mind. For he was a father to orphans in his love for them,
and a brother to the poor in his care for them. He was also a companion of mourners in his humble way of life,
and a friend of the holy in his excellent discernment. In his steadfastness, he was truly concerned for everyone's life.”
These, then, were the things they said as they wept over themselves, and they repeated such things as they lamented their own plight.
The following day, they hurried to conceal his pure body in a wooden coffin

right there inside his monastery, so that his holy body would not be torn apart by the hands of all the people, who crowded around in their love for him, seeking in their faith to receive grace from him.
Thus they accompanied him with psalms and hymns, bearing him solemnly in procession with due care, as far as the haven of the tomb at Qamtran.
In which the toil-worn ship of his blessed old age came to rest, carrying within it a great cargo of righteousness.
From it he distributes help to those who, in faith, ask his Lord in his name to attend to them through his faithful treasurer,
with a gift of mercy from the treasury of his compassion. For look: the sick are there and are healed; the healthy are there and are helped.
Demons too are there and are driven out; the distressed are there and are comforted. The poor too are there and are provided for,
and the rich too are enriched. For even his cold corpse is a spring of blessings,
through the fervor of the Spirit who rested in him. By his Lord’s permission, he had authority over the substance of his possessions,
so that from them he could readily dispense good things to all who approach him in need.
But he has gathered his wealth to himself in full, and all the labor of his races is kept completely safe with him,
until his body is raised and renewed, and his soul is adorned as a bride within it and becomes radiant, so that, complete in both, he may shine in glory
on the day of the glorious appearing of the Son of God, the Savior of all. May he, through the gift of his mercy, graciously make us all worthy
to stand at his right hand under the shelter of our victorious father’s peacemaking protection. And may our father speak boldly to his Lord on our behalf, joining himself with us:
“Here I am, my Lord, and the children you have given me. We worship you, we acknowledge your Father, and we glorify your Holy Spirit, both now and forever and ever. Amen.”
The writing of the triumphs of Mar Rabbula is finished.
The bishop.
